articles.title: Giant tunnel proposed to clean up Windermere's sewage problem
articles.summary: The plan would eliminate sewage spills into Windermere, blamed for turning the water green.
articles.content:
A £3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.

The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.

At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.

It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the £3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.

The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year.

Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant environmental infrastructure proposal aimed at eliminating sewage pollution in Windermere, England's largest lake. This project has broad environmental and public health benefits, protecting a UNESCO World Heritage site and improving water quality for millions of visitors and local residents. The proposal is detailed, backed by stakeholders, and addresses a major pollution problem with measurable positive impact.

**What happened** – A proposal costing £3.6 billion has been made to build a tunnel up to 12 miles (19 kilometers) long. This tunnel would carry sewage away from Windermere instead of letting it flow into the lake. The plan is supported by the local water company, United Utilities, and environmental campaigners. The government will now decide whether to approve the project and its cost.

**Impact** – If built, the tunnel would stop sewage spills into Windermere, helping to keep the water clean and clear. This would protect the lake’s natural beauty and improve the experience for visitors and local people. It would also help the lake’s ecosystem by reducing harmful algae blooms caused by sewage pollution.

**What's next step** – The government will review the proposal to decide if the tunnel project should move forward. If approved, it could lead to construction starting in the coming years. This project might also serve as a model for protecting other important lakes and rivers from pollution.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new tunnel plan could end sewage pollution in Windermere, protecting the lake’s water quality and the environment for millions of visitors and residents.

articles.title: Estate records 'abundance' of wildlife despite drought
articles.summary: Wimpole's "long-term approach to nature recovery" has seen more than 5,000 species recorded.
articles.content:
A country house and farming estate in one of England's driest and most nature-depleted areas has an "abundance" of wildlife with more than 5,000 species recorded, the National Trust has said.

Rare species, including barbastelle bats, great crested newts and corn buntings, have been spotted at the Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire in the last six years.

General manager David Hassall said the number was "remarkable in any landscape, but particularly here in Cambridgeshire, where wildlife is facing the combined pressures of habitat loss and increasingly hot, dry conditions".

The government said the East was one of seven UK areas in drought, external, with hosepipe bans in force across parts of the region.

The charity said 5,242 species were recorded across the estate's parkland, farmland, woodland and wetlands.

Hassall said the number "reflects five decades of careful stewardship and shows that nature can flourish alongside farming, public access and heritage conservation".
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant positive environmental impact where a long-term nature recovery effort on the Wimpole Estate has led to an abundance of wildlife, including rare species, despite drought conditions. This demonstrates successful conservation and habitat restoration with broad ecological benefits.

This includes rare creatures like barbastelle bats, great crested newts, and corn buntings. The National Trust, which manages the estate, says this is a big achievement.

**Impact** – This is important because the area is one of the driest in England and is currently facing drought with water restrictions. articles.title: The British island where red squirrels are thriving
articles.summary: Conservationists say that, with red squirrels dwindling in the UK, Jersey is an "important refuge".
articles.content:
With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England, one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.

Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.

Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.

There have some strongholds in England, external, particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland, external.

However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".

He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.

"That is actually really special for them."

Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.

However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.

The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey, external tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the thriving population of endangered red squirrels on Jersey, which serves as an important refuge due to the absence of invasive grey squirrels. This represents a meaningful conservation success with broad ecological significance and public interest, supported by detailed context about the species' status and local efforts.

**What happened** – On the island of Jersey, red squirrels are doing well. This is because Jersey has no grey squirrels, so the red squirrels there do not face the deadly virus. Although red squirrels were brought to Jersey in 1885 and are not originally from there, they have lived on the island so long that they have become a natural part of the environment.

**Impact** – Jersey is now an important safe place for red squirrels, helping keep the species alive in the UK. Visitors to Jersey often want to see these squirrels because they are rare in many other places. The island’s success shows how protecting animals from threats like invasive species can help endangered wildlife recover.

**What’s next step** – Conservation groups and the island’s National Trust will continue to protect the red squirrels and promote Jersey as a place to see them. This might inspire similar efforts elsewhere to save red squirrels and other animals.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Jersey island offers a rare safe home where endangered red squirrels are thriving without the threat of invasive grey squirrels.

articles.title: A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre, a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete, a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, […]
The post A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre, a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise.

The company has developed Mosscrete, a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology, and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands.

How moss takes hold

Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall, which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one.

The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions.

Eight buildings, different tests

In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one.

A 300-square-meter (about 3,230-square-foot) noise barrier in Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, is being used to test passive greening: moss growing from natural moisture alone, no watering involved. The porous structure of moss may also help absorb sound, which makes the noise barrier a natural fit for the technology.

A 260-square-meter (about 2,800-square-foot) social housing facade in Purmerend was one of the first practical applications. Traditional greening options were rejected there as too expensive and maintenance-heavy, and the project helped Respyre work out how bioreceptive facades are best designed and applied. In Haarlem, a 313-square-meter (about 3,370-square-foot) commercial renovation combined Mosscrete with insulation, aiming to both green the facade and improve thermal performance. Research published in June 2026 in the journal Science of the Total Environment found the effect is moisture-dependent: wet moss creates a cooling effect through evaporation, while dry moss can overheat in direct sunlight.

In Amsterdam, the technology is being tested on bridge piers where graffiti has been a persistent problem. Moss-covered surfaces are less appealing as targets, and since the site has no irrigation, the project is also tracking how moss develops under ordinary conditions of rain, shade, and humidity.

Designing for change

Respyre is betting on a different idea of what building materials should do. Most are made to resist change, to stay gray and sealed for decades. Mosscrete is made for the opposite: it works best when moss gradually takes over.

Urban greening helps manage stormwater and heat in dense cities, and there’s evidence it supports local biodiversity too. But a building slowly covered in moss doesn’t look like neglect. It looks like something is alive there.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.personality_title: Dutch startup creates concrete that grows moss without soil or watering

Depuis son lancement, Mosscrete a été utilisé sur huit bâtiments en Belgique et aux Pays-Bas, comme des entrepôts, des barrières anti-bruit et des logements sociaux.
